per_run.approach_summary: Profiled all 106 anonymized features, including cardinality, missingness, marginal AUC, and class balance. Compared standardized logistic regression, ExtraTrees, LightGBM, and CatBoost with 5-fold stratified CV. Random CV favored LightGBM (AUC 0.9271), but the temporally/separately sampled confirmation set strongly favored CatBoost: the baseline depth-7 CatBoost scored 0.9367 versus 0.8995-0.9030 for tested LightGBM variants; LightGBM/CatBoost blends were worse. Used all 20 permitted confirmation calls to test capacity, regularization, and ensembles. Depths 5, 6, 8, and 9 scored 0.9201, 0.9333, 0.9324, and 0.9361 respectively. The selected 70/30 rank ensemble of depth-7 and depth-9 CatBoost models scored best at 0.9380. Retrained both on all 5,000 research rows and applied the same rank ensemble separately to transfer and real_test rows.

Profiled all 106 anonymized features, missingness, cardinalities, univariate signal, and research-to-confirmation drift. Compared regularized LightGBM, ExtraTrees, and CatBoost with five-fold stratified out-of-fold evaluation. Random CV favored LightGBM (0.9203), but local confirmation favored CatBoost: baseline depth 6 scored 0.9274 and depth 8 scored 0.9310; depths 9/10 fell to 0.9292/0.9289, explicit low-cardinality categorical handling scored 0.9259, and blends did not improve on 0.9310. The final approach is the same five-fold depth-8 CatBoost ensemble used for that score, excluding row_id. I attacked the result as possible contiguous-holdout or single-feature leakage: forward backtests were weaker (AUC 0.753/0.809/0.824 with 3000/3500/4000 training rows) but improved with sample size; importance was distributed (largest feature about 10%, top ten about 58%); key-feature marginal shifts were generally small; row_id was never used; and seed/capacity/model blends did not reveal a brittle peak. The attack raises variance/drift caution but did not provide convincing evidence of a confirmation-only shortcut, so the tested depth-8 ensemble was retained.

Profiled all 106 anonymized features, including cardinality, missingness, univariate signal, and train/target distribution overlap. Compared logistic, ExtraTrees, random forest, histogram boosting, LightGBM, and CatBoost with stratified five-fold validation. Tree boosting dominated; confirmation feedback favored numeric CatBoost despite locally stronger histogram models. The final approach adds label-free population frequency encodings for the four card-like high-cardinality columns and the amount-like column, averages five early-stopped CatBoost and five class-weighted LightGBM folds, and blends their rank predictions 70/30. Frequency-aware CatBoost scored 0.9341 on confirmation; the selected CatBoost/LightGBM rank blend scored 0.9357. Native categorical treatment was tested but was weaker (0.9281), and a fixed-iteration full-data refit also trailed (0.9321).

Explored all 106 features for cardinality, missingness, nonlinear univariate signal, repeated values, cross-split overlap, row-order effects, and grouped structure. Benchmarked logistic regression, Extra Trees, LightGBM, and CatBoost under five-fold stratified and blocked validation. Random-fold AUCs were about 0.828, 0.903, 0.922, and 0.913 respectively; repeated exact amount and identifier/count values were the main additional structure. Confirmation probes scored 0.9072 for LightGBM, 0.9090 for Extra Trees, 0.9279 for the initial categorical model, 0.9395 after selected count/key categorical treatment, and 0.9427 for its four-seed ensemble. A 90% rank of that ensemble plus 10% rank of LightGBM was best at 0.9432; an eight-seed extension fell to 0.9426. I attacked the best result as possible confirmation-specific entity/value memorization and temporal drift. Its AUC remained 0.8635 on blocked folds and 0.8623 when validation groups had disjoint primary identifiers. Mean seen-category coverage was nearly identical in confirmation and transfer (0.9831 versus 0.9816); real test was more shifted but retained 0.9717 mean coverage. Adversarial dataset classifiers found mild confirmation shift (AUC 0.5646), moderate transfer shift (0.5978), and stronger real-test shift (0.7363), so I retained the 10% numeric booster as a robustness component. The evidence did not support confirmation-only leakage, and the exact attacked four-seed categorical plus numeric rank blend was applied unchanged to transfer and real_test.

DATA STRUCTURE FOUND (all discovery done on research.json only; features are anonymized).
106 features, 5000 labeled rows, 4.78% positive (239 pos). I first reverse-engineered the
schema rather than modelling blind.

1) Exact count/amount pairing. Hashing each column's zero-pattern over the 5000 research rows
   gave 26 pairs of columns with byte-identical zero masks, e.g. (x_016,x_047), (x_097,x_042),
   (x_054,x_081), (x_072,x_094). Each pair is a "number of events of type k" column and its
   matching "total amount for type k" column, so amount/count is a well-defined per-event
   average. Nonzero-set containment showed two roll-up families: x_043 is a super-total over
   {x_042,x_044..x_053} with count total x_098, and x_082 is a super-total over
   {x_081,x_083..x_096} (with x_089 itself a roll-up of x_088,x_090). The roll-ups are not exact
   sums, so the sub-categories overlap rather than partition.

2) Cluster structure. Average-linkage clustering on 1-|corr| of log1p features split the
   low-cardinality count block cleanly into a COMMON cluster
   {x_000,x_002,x_004,x_005,x_006,x_009,x_010,x_013} (mutual corr 0.85-0.99) and a RARE cluster
   {x_001,x_003,x_008,x_011,x_012} which also pulls in {x_077,x_078,x_079}. It also recovered
   parallel severity triples across families: (x_017,x_018,x_019)~(x_048,x_049,x_050)~
   (x_068..x_070)/(x_091..x_093), and (x_020..x_022)~(x_051..x_053)~(x_071..x_074)/(x_094..x_096).

3) x_015 behaves as an exposure/size denominator (never zero, heavy-tailed). Counts divided by
   x_015 are far more informative than raw counts, and 8 of the top 20 gain features are such
   rates.

WHY THE MODEL WORKS. The single highest-gain feature is the share of RARE-cluster activity among
all small counts (sum_rare/sum_small). The population splits into two subpopulations that behave
very differently: rows with any RARE-cluster count (n=1277) have a 12.7% positive rate and are
easy (subgroup OOF AUC 0.96); rows with none (n=3723) have a 2.1% rate and are hard (0.86). A
second strong axis is the low-cardinality code x_104: positive rate 3.2% at <=150, 17.8% in
(150,185], 27% above. Most of the model's discriminating power is the interaction of rare-share,
rare-share-per-exposure, and these codes.

FEATURE SETS BUILT. raw (106); fe1 (221) = raw + 26 per-event averages + family shares + nonzero
breadth counts + x_015-normalised rates + selected count ratios; fe1f = fe1 + 7 transductive
frequency encodings; fe2 (318) = fe1 + cluster-level sums/shares/rates.

DISTRIBUTION SHIFT (this drove several decisions). Adversarial validation: research vs
confirmation 0.581, research vs transfer 0.586, confirmation vs transfer 0.571 -- the last is the
noise floor for this setup, so those three splits are effectively exchangeable. research vs
real_test is 0.73-0.77, i.e. real_test is genuinely a different population (higher RARE-cluster
counts, wider x_015 range, top shift drivers x_014, x_015, x_102, x_103, x_013). I tested
importance weighting (density ratio from the adversarial model, clipped at the 99th pct) with a
stress split: train on the half of research least like real_test, test on the half most like it.
Weighting did NOT help (raw 0.8568 plain vs 0.8542 weighted; fe1 0.8625 vs 0.8611), so I dropped
it. The same test showed the ratio/share features transfer at least as well as raw features
(0.8625 vs 0.8568), which is why fe1 rather than raw is the ensemble's backbone.

WHAT HELPED. (a) fe1 over raw: 0.9186 -> 0.9232 at first, 0.9251 -> 0.9286 after tuning.
(b) Transductive frequency encoding: log-count of each row's value for
{x_102,x_103,x_104,x_105,x_015,x_014,x_004} within the 506,691-row real_test corpus, computed
identically for every split. This is a "how common is this profile in the population" signal and
was the single best late gain: 0.9279 -> 0.9309 with the lowest fold-to-fold variance of anything
tried. Widening it to all 53 high-cardinality columns (0.9299) or all 106 (0.9294) was worse.
(c) Blending across feature views and hyperparameters, and bagging over seeds (single-model CV
0.931 vs bagged OOF 0.938).

WHAT I TRIED AND REJECTED. fe2's 97 cluster aggregates hurt (0.9238 vs 0.9286) -- they dilute
colsample with redundant columns; it survives only as a small-weight diversity member. Explicit
stratified sub-models on the rare-cluster split gave 0.9284 vs 0.9281 global, i.e. the global
model already encodes the split. Exact-row multiplicity in real_test hurt (0.9257) even though
research rows that recur in real_test are genuinely lower risk (1.7% vs 5.0% positive) -- too few
support rows, and 48 real_test rows match a POSITIVE research row, so a hard duplicate override
would have been unsafe. Hyperparameter sweeps found the reference config near-optimal:
scale_pos_weight 5/20, lr 0.01 with 4000 trees, extra_trees, path_smooth, max_bin 511, L1, and
subsample 0.5 all landed at or below 0.928. Other model families were clearly weaker than
LightGBM (CatBoost 0.9078, RF 0.8994, ExtraTrees 0.8883, quantile-transformed logistic 0.8517)
and adding them to the blend lowered OOF, so the final ensemble is LightGBM-only.

FINAL MODEL. 21 LightGBM classifiers = 4 feature views (fe1f x3 hyperparameter settings weight
1.0/1.0/0.5, fe1 0.75, raw x2 0.75/0.5, fe2 0.5) x 3 seeds, each 1500 trees at lr 0.03, trained
on all 5000 research rows. Members are aggregated by weighted average of within-set percentile
ranks (min pairwise rank-corr 0.79, so the members are genuinely diverse), then the blended rank
is mapped monotonically onto the weighted-mean predicted-probability distribution so the emitted
numbers sit on a probability scale without changing the ordering.

CONFIRMATION FEEDBACK. 3 scorer calls. Call 1, first ensemble (no frequency encoding): 0.9210.
Call 2, final ensemble with frequency encoding: 0.9206. Call 3, same after the calibration map:
0.9206 (identical, confirming the map is monotone and bug-free). With ~1500 rows the standard
error on confirmation AUC is roughly 0.02, so it cannot resolve the ~0.003 differences my CV was
measuring -- I therefore used the confirmation set only as a sanity check against a gross
train/serve mismatch, and made every selection decision on 3-repeat 5-fold CV over the research
rows (fold-level SD ~0.002-0.003). The confirmation figure (0.921) sitting a little below the
bagged OOF (0.938) is the expected optimism of an OOF estimate that is itself an average of
fold models, not evidence of a leak.

CAVEAT I WANT ON THE RECORD. real_test is measurably a different population from the rows I could
validate on, and nothing available to me scores it. I expect transfer.json performance to land
near the confirmation figure, and real_test performance to be lower; the shift-robustness choices
above (ratio features, no importance weighting, population-level frequency encoding, heavy
blending) were made to limit that gap, but they are untested on the actual target.

DATA. 5,000 labeled rows (4.78% positive, 239 positives), 106 anonymized features, plus
1,500 confirmation, 1,500 transfer (row_ids 0-7999 = one contiguous pool) and 506,691
real_test rows (row_ids 1,000,000+, a separate and larger pool).

STRUCTURE FOUND. (a) 26 exact count->amount column pairs, identified by columns having
byte-identical zero patterns (e.g. x_017/x_048, x_097/x_042). (b) A nested "tier"
hierarchy among the sparse counts: presence of a rarer column strictly implies presence of
commoner ones (319 such implications; e.g. x_017 => x_019 => x_018), i.e. cumulative
severity counters. (c) Five sparse counts (x_001, x_003, x_008, x_011, x_012) occur only in
11 of the 32 possible presence patterns, and the pattern is strongly predictive: 00000
(74% of rows) is 2.1% positive, 01000 is 12.4%, 11111 is 13.8%, 11110 is 15/15. The same
11 patterns, with shifted frequencies, appear in real_test. (d) x_102 is a fine-grained
grouping key (13,244 values over the full pool) nested inside x_103, x_104 and x_105
(>99.5% single-parent), i.e. a geography/organisation-style hierarchy. x_104 is effectively
categorical: value 150 (87% of rows) is 3.1% positive, value 185 (10%) is 18.0%, and those
frequencies match between research and real_test.

WHY THE MODEL WORKS. Best single feature reaches only 0.709 AUC while the model reaches
~0.93, so essentially all of the performance is interaction-driven. Two mechanisms carry
it. First, the sparse-count presence pattern: it splits the population into a majority
subgroup with no rare claim types and a minority with them, and the model discriminates
well inside *both* (OOF AUC 0.873 on the 3,723 all-zero rows, 0.960 on the other 1,277) --
so it is not merely separating the subgroups. Second, genuine peer-group risk carried by
x_102: some x_102 groups are drastically elevated (one group is 14/14 positive, another
12/26). I tested whether this is real or memorisation by building OOF predictions from a
model with x_102/x_103/x_105 removed and permutation-testing the within-x_102 clustering of
the residuals: z = 6.4, p < 0.0025. The group effect survives conditioning on every other
feature, so it is real structure, not an artifact.

WHAT DID NOT WORK (all tested with 4-5 repeat 5-fold CV; raw baseline 0.9346-0.9365):
pair ratios / shares / totals (0.9218 mid, 0.9137 full block); transductive peer-group
features built from the 506k unlabeled pool -- group means and per-row deviations from the
x_102/x_103/x_105 peer profile (0.9350-0.9363, i.e. noise); hierarchically-smoothed
out-of-fold target encoding of the x_102 hierarchy at alpha 5/20/60 (0.9262-0.9278, clearly
worse). CatBoost 0.901, RandomForest 0.917, ExtraTrees 0.894, logistic-on-quantiles 0.843;
blending any of them into the LGBM ensemble was neutral-to-negative. A 40-config random
search over LightGBM plateaued at 0.925-0.931 with no config beating the hand-found one --
the whole region is noise-dominated at 239 positives.

FINAL APPROACH. 5 LightGBM configurations (num_leaves 31-127, lr 0.03-0.05, 800-2000
trees, subsample+colsample) x 3 seeds = 15 models on the 106 RAW features, retrained on all
5,000 research rows, combined by rank-averaging. OOF 0.9365; the CV-argmax pair (C1+C4)
scored 0.9380, but that 0.0015 is far below the +/-0.006 seed-to-seed noise, so I kept the
5-config average as the less CV-overfit choice. Applied unchanged to confirmation, transfer
and real_test.

CONFIRMATION SCORES (3 calls). Call 1, single config x 5 seeds, all features: 0.9065.
Call 2, same but with x_102/x_103/x_105 deleted: 0.9042. Call 3, final 5-config ensemble:
0.9091. The ordering matches CV but every gap is small; with ~72 positives in 1,500 rows the
AUC standard error is ~0.02, so I deliberately treated confirmation as a sanity check and
never tuned against it.

ATTACKING MY OWN APPROACH. The strongest sceptical case is that x_102/x_103/x_105 are the
model's 2nd/3rd/5th most-split features yet have near-zero univariate AUC -- the exact
signature of a high-cardinality ID being memorised. Deleting them costs 0.024 in CV
(0.9346 -> 0.9101) but only 0.0023 on confirmation, a 10x discrepancy that looks damning.
I pursued it four ways. (1) I mirrored the deployment setup exactly: 12 repeated 3500/1500
splits, train on 3500, measure the paired all-vs-nogeo AUC difference on the held-out 1500.
The difference has mean +0.0145 with sd 0.0145 and ranges from -0.007 to +0.038; 33% of
splits land at or below the +0.0023 confirmation observed. So confirmation does not
contradict CV -- 1,500-row AUC is simply that noisy (absolute AUC across those splits ranged
0.874-0.967, which also explains the CV 0.93 vs confirmation 0.91 gap). (2) Group overlap is
not a fold artifact: the mean number of research rows sharing a row's x_102 value is 22.6
for a research row, 22.0 for a confirmation row and 19.5 for a real_test row, and 76% of
real_test rows have their x_102 present in research -- the group signal is as available at
deployment as in CV. (3) Shift-stress: I trained an adversarial classifier separating
research from real_test (AUC 0.774; top drivers x_102, x_015, x_103), split research into
its least- and most-real_test-like halves, trained on the former and tested on the latter.
Averaged over 3 adversarial seeds the geo features helped by the same margin on the shifted
half (0.8626 vs 0.8506) as on a random half (0.8994 vs 0.8876) -- the degradation under
shift is +0.037 for every candidate, so the geo block is not shift-fragile. (4) Coincidental
overlap: 22 confirmation rows are exact feature duplicates of research rows, and all 22 of
the matching research rows are negatives, so duplicate leakage cannot be inflating the
score. The attack therefore failed and I kept the geo features.

Two residual weaknesses I could not eliminate, stated honestly. First, the row_id ordering
of the 0-7999 pool is not fully shuffled -- rows 2000-2250 are 16% positive against a 4.8%
base rate, and similar blocks recur throughout the pool (including inside confirmation and
transfer). Observations are therefore clustered, the effective sample size is below 5,000,
and random-fold CV is mildly optimistic; that is part of why CV (0.9365) sits above
confirmation (0.9091). Because the blocks recur in all three splits it is not a
research-versus-confirmation composition artifact, so I did not correct for it beyond
widening my own uncertainty. Second, real_test is a genuinely shifted population, not a
prevalence-shifted copy: implied prevalence back-solved from single-feature means is
mutually inconsistent (0.06 to 0.72, some negative), and features like x_014, which is
negatively associated with the target, are *higher* in real_test. I expect real_test AUC
around 0.86-0.90 rather than the 0.93 CV figure, based on the shift-stress result.
